title: Reclaiming a Vision of Humane Schooling
author: Alicia Stoller
summary: In this guest essay for Benjamin Riley's Build Cognitive Resonance, Alicia Stoller, a former preschool teacher, director and graduate instructor, argues that fear of an uncertain future pushes schools and parents to define education only as armour for the future, at the cost of children's present humanity. She says this fear opens the door to predatory versions of school that profit from anxiety, and uses Alpha School as an example of a gap between stated values like joy and actual practices. She then offers six anchor points for humane schooling: a joyous spirit of exploration, a wild embrace of wonder and imagination, deep empathy, diligence and fortitude, tolerance for uncertainty, and love for the world as it is and as it could be. Her closing claim is that the values adults espouse are credible only if their present actions bear them out.
points: Fear of the future can trap adults into treating school only as preparation, sacrificing children's present lives.
Fear creates openings for predatory schools and ed-tech companies that use trusted words such as joy and literacy to disguise profit-driven aims.
Alpha School is cited as an example where stated values of joy and being valued clash with practices such as monitoring heart rates and tracking emotions.
The humane vision includes joy, wonder, empathy, diligent effort, tolerance for uncertainty and love for the world as it is and could be.
Productive struggle does not have to oppose joy or a child's dignity, and adults must model the values they claim.
quotes: But when fear overwhelms us, preoccupation with the future can become a trap. And in trying to protect our children, we may find we’ve forfeited their childhood.
When we view education solely as armor that will protect our children from hardship or scarcity, we risk sacrificing their full humanity today, and the possibility of a less dire tomorrow.
Sometimes, though, articulated values only serve to provide a virtue-signaling haze meant to obscure less virtuous goals — usually some external profit or power.
Monitoring a student’s heart rate while they are publicly criticized by their parents, or using software to track and correct a child’s emotions, does not instill joy or make kids feel valued.
The deepest learning begins in wonder, not in the cold pursuit of achievement.
But a tolerance for productive struggle doesn’t have to operate in opposition to joy, wonder, empathy, or a child’s own dignity.
The way in which we value children as they stand before us instructs them in who they are permitted to become, and in the values they should uphold themselves.

Children are paying constant, close attention to the world around them. The values we espouse for their future are only credible when our actions, as the adults in their lives, bear those values out in the present.
